C6.1.q: Why does changing a wave's outline change how it sounds?
options: A different outline is a different set of harmonics
A different outline makes the wave repeat more often
A different outline makes the whole wave much louder
A different outline lets a filter remove more harmonics
C6.1.why: Warp changes the wave's outline, and a different outline is a different set of harmonics.

C6.1.q: How is warp different from a filter?
options: Warp removes harmonics; a filter can only add them
Warp changes the note; a filter changes the loudness
Warp can add harmonics; a filter can only take them away
Warp needs a second oscillator; a filter does not
C6.1.why: Warp changes the wave's outline, so it can add harmonics, while a filter can only take them away.

C6.1.q: Why does the note stay the same when you turn warp up?
options: The wave still repeats just as often
The filter holds the pitch in place
Hold is switched on for the note
The new harmonics are too quiet to hear
C6.1.why: Pitch comes from how often the wave repeats, and warp does not change that.

C6.1.q: How does warp change the outline of a wave?
options: It mixes in a second oscillator's wave
It reads the wave at an uneven speed
It removes harmonics above a set point
It turns the wave's level up and down
C6.1.why: Warp reads the wave at an uneven speed, which changes its outline.

C6.1.q: You hold a sine, set Warp to Bend and turn the amount up. What do you hear?
options: The tone dropping to a lower note
The tone growing brighter and more nasal
The tone getting duller and softer
The tone fading slowly to silence
C6.1.why: Bend changes the outline of the wave, so new harmonics appear and the tone gets brighter and more nasal.

C6.1.q: You set a saw to Mirror at 100%. What happens to the sound?
options: It turns brighter and buzzier, like a pulse
It jumps up to a higher note
It becomes a pure tone with one harmonic
It turns soft and hollow, like a triangle
C6.1.why: Read forwards then backwards, the saw's outline becomes a triangle, and a new outline means different harmonics.

C6.1.q: A saw is on Mirror at 100%. You bring the amount down to about half. What do you get?
options: A pure sine with one harmonic
The same sound, an octave higher
A saw with a filter closing on it
Something between a saw and a triangle
C6.1.why: At about half, the turn-around point has moved, so the wave sits between a saw and a triangle.

C6.2.q: Why does the pitch hold when sync reads the wave faster?
options: The wave is read forwards and then backwards
The wave starts again at the end of every cycle
A macro keeps pulling the pitch back down
The extra copies are too quiet to hear
C6.2.why: Sync restarts the wave every time the cycle ends, so the cycle is as long as before.

C6.2.q: You hold a low note on Sync and turn Warp amount slowly all the way up. What does the scope show?
options: Extra teeth squeezing into each cycle
The teeth spreading further apart
The wave smoothing into a sine
The wave growing taller each cycle
C6.2.why: Sync reads the wave faster, so more than one copy of the wave fits inside each cycle.

C6.2.q: What makes sync sound torn and bright?
options: A filter opens wider as the amount is turned up
A second oscillator plays slightly out of tune with the first
The wave gets louder until its top is cut flat
The last copy of the wave is cut short, leaving a sharp edge
C6.2.why: The cut-short copy leaves a sharp edge, and sharp edges are bright.

C6.2.q: As you turn the Sync amount up, what happens to the harmonics?
options: They all fade out from the top down
They all slide up to a higher note
A strong peak sweeps up through them
They stay the same and only get louder
C6.2.why: As the amount turns, the cut moves and a strong peak sweeps up through the harmonics.

C6.2.q: You want a clean saw exactly an octave higher, using Sync. Where do you set Warp amount?
options: All the way to the top
About halfway up the knob
About a third of the way up
Just a little above zero
C6.2.why: About a third of the way up, exactly two whole teeth fit in each cycle, so nothing is cut short.

C6.2.q: You want to play the sync sweep from one knob you can name. What do you do?
options: Send a macro to Warp amount and turn the macro
Leave Warp amount at full and play other notes
Change the shape from saw to sine and back
Switch Hold off and strike the key harder
C6.2.why: The sweep of the amount is the sound, so a macro sent to Warp amount lets you play it.

C6.3.q: What does Squeeze do to a square wave?
options: Makes it repeat faster, raising the pitch
Rounds off its corners, turning it into a sine
Makes the high part shorter, turning it into a pulse
Reads it forwards and then backwards
C6.3.why: Squeeze hurries through the first half, so the square's high part gets shorter and its pulse width changes.

options: How loud the high part of the wave is
How many harmonics the pulse contains
How often the pulse repeats each second
How much of each cycle the wave spends high
C6.3.why: Pulse width is how much of the cycle is spent high.

C6.3.q: How does a narrow pulse sound next to a square, and why?
options: Hollower, because the even harmonics are taken out
Thinner and more nasal, because even harmonics come in
Duller, because the high harmonics are filtered off
Lower, because the wave repeats less often
C6.3.why: A square has only odd harmonics, and narrowing the pulse lets the even ones in, which sounds thinner and more nasal.

C6.3.q: You hold a square and take Squeeze all the way to 100%. What is left?
options: A louder, fuller, heavier square
A thin, reedy buzz with much less body
A pure tone with a single harmonic
A hollow tone an octave lower
C6.3.why: At full amount the wave is a narrow spike, which sounds thin and reedy with much less body.

C6.3.q: You change the shape to Sine and sweep Squeeze from 0 to 100%. What do you hear?
options: A pure tone rising steadily to a higher note
A pure tone turning hollow, like a square
A pure tone that does not change at all
A pure tone leaning toward a saw, like a filter opening
C6.3.why: Squeezing a sine tilts it toward a saw, so it brightens as if a filter were opening.

options: Reshaping a wave by changing the speed it is read at
Reshaping a wave by turning its level up and down
Reshaping a wave by removing its even harmonics
Reshaping a wave by making it repeat more often
C6.3.why: Reshaping a wave by changing its reading speed, as Squeeze does, is known as phase distortion.

C6.3.q: What do you get by moving the pulse width slowly back and forth?
options: A steady rise and fall in the note's pitch
A tone that fades slowly away to silence
A clean jump up an octave and back
A rich, shifting tone, as in string and pad patches
C6.3.why: Slowly moving the pulse width gives a rich, animated tone.

C6.4.q: What happens when a pitch wobble is sped up until it is as fast as a note?
options: You stop hearing the pitch move and hear new harmonics
The vibrato gets wider and easier to hear
The note gets louder but keeps its tone
The note drops out and leaves a gap
C6.4.why: FM is pitch modulation so fast that it is heard as tone, not as movement.

C6.4.q: Oscillator B is switched off. Can it still be used for FM on oscillator A?
options: No: B must be switched on and heard first
Yes: B can shake A without being switched on
Only if B's level is turned all the way up
Only if B's shape is set to a saw
C6.4.why: B does the shaking and A is what you hear, so B does not have to be switched on.

C6.4.q: Your FM tone has become too hard and buzzy. What do you change?
options: Turn FM from B down
Switch oscillator B off
Turn FM from B up
Switch Hold off
C6.4.why: The FM amount sets how many new partials appear, so less amount gives a less bright tone.

C6.4.q: Where should B's pitch sit against A's for an FM tone to stay musical?
options: A few semitones above A, in between the octaves
Anywhere at all, as long as B is switched on
Anywhere at all, as long as the amount is low
At the same pitch, or a whole number of octaves away
C6.4.why: At the same pitch or a whole number of octaves away, the new partials land on harmonics.

C6.4.q: With FM on, you set B's Octave to 1. What happens to the new bars on the spectrum?
options: They are now twice as close together
They all disappear, leaving one bar
They are now twice as far apart
They stay in place but grow taller
C6.4.why: B's pitch against A's sets where the partials fall, and B is now twice as high.

C6.4.q: With FM on, B sits an octave and 6 semitones above A. Why does it clang?
options: The FM amount has been turned up too far
Oscillator B is now loud enough to be heard
The new partials no longer line up with the note's harmonics
The envelope is making the note far too short
C6.4.why: B's pitch against A's sets where the new partials fall, and in between whole octaves they miss the harmonics.

C6.4.q: How do you make a bell that starts bright and mellows as it rings out?
options: Send a slow LFO to oscillator A's pitch
Send an envelope to the FM amount
Turn the FM amount up and leave it
Switch oscillator B on and raise its level
C6.4.why: An envelope on the FM amount gives a bright strike that mellows to a pure tone.

C6.5.q: How does ring modulation combine oscillators A and B?
options: It multiplies one signal by the other
It adds one signal to the other
It plays one signal after the other
It uses one signal to filter the other
C6.5.why: Ring modulation multiplies one signal by another.

C6.5.q: Two pure tones are ring modulated at full amount. What comes out?
options: Both original tones, a little louder
The original tones plus two new ones
Only the lower tone, an octave down
Only their sum and their difference
C6.5.why: Two pure tones give one tone at the sum of their frequencies and one at the difference, and the originals are gone.

C6.5.q: A and B are sines at the same pitch. You turn Ring from B all the way up. What do you hear?
options: The note drops down an octave
The note gets twice as loud
Two notes slightly out of tune
The note jumps up an octave
C6.5.why: The sum of two equal frequencies is double, and the difference is zero, which is no sound.

C6.5.q: Ring is at 100% and your own note has gone, leaving a gap. How do you get it back?
options: Bring Ring from B down to about half
Change the two shapes to Saw
Set B's Semitone higher
Switch Hold off and on again
C6.5.why: At about half, your own note returns in the middle with the two new tones either side.

C6.5.q: With Ring at full, you change both shapes to Saw. Why is the tone so dense?
options: The two saws are now heard at twice the level
Saws switch ring modulation over to FM
Each saw adds a tone an octave below
Every harmonic of A pairs with every harmonic of B
C6.5.why: With richer waves, every harmonic of one pairs with every harmonic of the other.

C6.5.q: With two sines, how does FM differ from ring modulation as you turn it up?
options: Ring keeps adding pairs of partials; FM makes just one pair
FM changes the note's loudness; ring changes its pitch
FM keeps adding pairs of partials; ring makes just one pair
Ring needs B to be heard; FM works with B off
C6.5.why: FM makes many pairs of partials as it rises, while ring modulation makes one pair per pair of harmonics.

C6.C.q: The hidden sound no longer contains the note being played. What should you suspect?
options: Sync
Ring modulation
Bend
Squeeze
C6.C.why: Ring modulation removes the played note and leaves new tones in its place.

C6.C.q: The hidden sound's added brightness is smooth, not torn. Which should you try?
options: Sync or bend
Sync or squeeze
Bend or squeeze
Sync only
C6.C.why: A smooth brightness points to bend or squeeze, while a torn, vowel-like one is sync.

C6.C.q: In an FM round, the new partials are further apart than yours. What do you change?
options: The pitch of oscillator B
The level of oscillator B
The FM amount
The warp amount
C6.C.why: With FM, B's pitch sets how far apart the new partials are.

C7.1.q: Why does distortion make a sound brighter?
options: It turns up the high harmonics that were already there
It takes away the low harmonics below a set point
It reshapes the wave, and a new shape means new harmonics
It plays a second, higher note on top
C7.1.why: Distortion reshapes a signal that is too big to fit, and the changed shape has new harmonics.

C7.1.q: Warp and distortion both add harmonics. Where does distortion do its work?
options: On the finished sound
Inside the oscillator, at the source
Only on the highest harmonics
Only on the start of each note
C7.1.why: Distortion adds brightness as warp does, but it is applied to the finished sound.

C7.1.q: You switch Distortion on, set to Soft clip, over a sine. What do you hear and see?
options: A harsher tone, with the tops cut dead flat
A warmer, fuller tone, with the tops rounded off
A gritty fizz, with the wave turned into steps
A thinner tone, with the wave made much smaller
C7.1.why: Soft clip bends the part that sticks out over, so the tops are rounded and the tone is warmer and fuller.

C7.1.q: On Soft clip, you turn Drive up past 80% on a sine. What is the wave pushed toward?
options: A staircase made of coarse steps
A square: flat on top, steep at the sides
A triangle with gently sloping sides
A smaller sine with the same outline
C7.1.why: High drive on soft clip pushes the sine toward a square, flat on top and steep at the sides.

C7.1.q: At the same drive, you change from Soft clip to Hard clip. What changes?
options: It sounds warmer, and the tops are rounded
It sounds quieter, and the wave is smaller
It sounds harsher, and the tops are cut flat
It sounds purer, and the new bars go
C7.1.why: Hard clip cuts the part that sticks out dead flat with sharp corners, which sounds harsher.

C7.1.q: On Fold, you sweep Drive slowly up. What happens to the tone?
options: It gets steadily brighter and nothing else changes
It turns into a gritty fizz made of steps
It gets steadily warmer and fuller, then stops
Harmonics rise and fall, giving a metallic, shifting tone
C7.1.why: Fold turns the part that sticks out back the way it came, so harmonics rise and fall as the wave folds again and again.

C7.1.q: On the scope the smooth wave has become a staircase. Which type is on?
options: Soft clip
Crush
Hard clip
Fold
C7.1.why: Crush rounds every value to a coarse grid of steps, which looks like a staircase.

C7.1.q: You want the weight of the clean sound with some distorted edge. What do you do?
options: Turn Drive all the way up
Turn Drive all the way down
Turn Mix all the way up
Turn Mix down to about half
C7.1.why: Mix blends the clean sound back in with the distorted one.

C7.2.q: Cutting High on the EQ made the sound duller but not muffled. Why?
options: The high harmonics are quieter, not gone
The low harmonics were boosted to match
The EQ only works on the middle band
The high harmonics were removed past a point
C7.2.why: An EQ turns a region down by a set amount, while a filter removes everything past a point.

C7.2.q: You switch the EQ on with every band at 0 dB. What do you hear?
options: No change at all
A slightly brighter sound
A slightly thinner sound
A slightly quieter sound
C7.2.why: An EQ only turns a region up or down by the amount you choose, and here every amount is zero.

C7.2.q: On an EQ, what are a cut and a boost?
options: A cut turns a band up; a boost turns it down
A cut removes a band; a boost adds a new one
A cut turns a band down; a boost turns it up
A cut moves a band lower; a boost moves it higher
C7.2.why: Turning a band down is called a cut and turning it up a boost.

C7.2.q: A sound is too thin and needs more weight at the bottom. What do you do?
options: Cut the low band
Boost the high band
Boost the low band
Cut the middle band
C7.2.why: The low band turns the bottom end up or down, and boosting it makes the sound heavier.

C7.2.q: You want to turn up one group of harmonics partway up the sound. Which band can you aim there?
options: The low band, by moving its frequency
The high band, by moving its frequency
Any band, as all three can move
The middle band, by moving its frequency
C7.2.why: The EQ has three bands, and the middle one is the band that can be moved.

C7.2.q: You boost one band a lot and sweep its frequency slowly. What do you hear?
options: A peak travelling through the sound, picking out groups of harmonics
The whole sound getting steadily louder and brighter all over
The note sliding slowly up to a higher pitch and back
The high harmonics being removed past a slowly moving point
C7.2.why: A swept boost is a peak that picks out one group of harmonics after another.

C7.2.q: What is the usual way to find and fix a boxy part of a sound?
options: Cut Low and High until only the boxy part is left
Boost a band a lot, sweep it to find the part, then cut
Cut a band fully, then sweep until the sound goes quiet
Boost all three bands, then turn the level down
C7.2.why: A big boost swept across the range makes the problem jump out, and then you set the amount you want.

C7.3.q: The threshold is set so high that no note reaches it. What does the compressor do?
options: It turns every note down equally
It turns down only the soft notes
It turns down only the start of each note
Nothing: no note is turned down
C7.3.why: A compressor only turns down what goes over the threshold.

C7.3.q: The compressor is on, but hard notes still stick out. What makes it turn them down more firmly?
options: Turning Threshold up to 0 dB
Turning Make-up up
Turning Ratio up
Turning Release up
C7.3.why: The ratio says how firmly the compressor turns down whatever goes over the threshold.

C7.3.q: With the compressor on, you play a hard note and then a soft one. What does “Turning down by” show?
options: More for the soft note than for the hard one
More for the hard note than for the soft one
The same amount for each note
Zero for each of the notes
C7.3.why: Hard notes go further over the threshold, so they are pulled down a long way and soft ones much less.

C7.3.q: After compressing, you turn Make-up up. What happens to the soft notes?
options: They end up much louder than before
They stay as quiet as before
They are turned down more than hard notes
They get a sharper front than hard notes
C7.3.why: Make-up gain brings the level back up, which lifts the quiet parts.

C7.3.q: What does the compressor's Release set?
options: How quickly it clamps down at first
How quickly it lets go afterwards
How firmly it turns the signal down
How loud a note must be to be turned down
C7.3.why: Attack is how quickly the compressor clamps down, and release is how quickly it lets go afterwards.

C7.3.q: Which setting lets the very start of a hard note through at full level?
options: A fast attack
A fast release
A slow attack
A higher ratio
C7.3.why: With a slow attack the start gets through before the compressor catches up.

C7.4.q: You switch Chorus on over one thin saw. What does it become?
options: Louder and harsher
Duller and softer
Wide and shimmering
Shorter and sharper
C7.4.why: Drifting copies of the sound make one thin saw wide and shimmering.

C7.4.q: Why do a chorus's copies drift flat and sharp against the original?
options: Each copy comes from an extra detuned oscillator
Their delays keep changing, which shifts the pitch slightly
Each copy is passed through a moving filter
Their levels keep changing, which sounds like pitch
C7.4.why: A chorus keeps changing each copy's delay, and a changing delay raises or lowers the pitch a little.

C7.4.q: With Depth at 0, what does the chorus sound like?
options: A gentle swirl that moves slowly
A fast wobble that sounds out of tune
No effect: only the original sound
A hollow, static colour with no movement
C7.4.why: Depth is how far the copies drift, so at 0 they sit still and give a fixed, hollow colour.

C7.4.q: The chorus wobbles so fast it starts to sound out of tune. What do you change?
options: Turn Rate up
Turn Rate down
Turn Mix up
Turn Depth up
C7.4.why: Rate is how fast the copies drift, and a slow rate gives a gentle swirl.

C7.4.q: You want the strongest swirl from the chorus. Where do you set Mix?
options: Around the middle
All the way up
All the way down
Just above zero
C7.4.why: The swirl is strongest when Mix is around the middle.

C7.4.q: What do chorus and unison have in common?
options: Echoes of one signal, evenly spaced, dying slowly away
Extra harmonics, added by reshaping the wave's outline
Higher harmonics, turned down by a set amount
Nearly identical signals, slightly out of tune, beating together
C7.4.why: Both are nearly identical signals, slightly out of tune, beating against each other.

C7.4.q: How is chorus different from unison?
options: Chorus is applied afterwards to the whole sound; unison is inside each note
Chorus is inside each note; unison is applied afterwards to the whole sound
Chorus changes only the pitch; unison changes only the loudness of each note
Chorus adds echoes after each note; unison adds a long smooth wash
C7.4.why: Unison is extra oscillators inside each note, and chorus is applied afterwards to everything at once.

C7.5.q: You want a longer gap between one echo and the next. What do you change?
options: Turn Time down
Turn Feedback up
Turn Feedback down
Turn Time up
C7.5.why: Time is how much later the delay plays the sound back, so it sets the gap between echoes.

C7.5.q: You want exactly one echo after each note. What do you set?
options: Feedback to about 75%
Time to half a beat
Feedback to 0
Time to about 60 ms
C7.5.why: Feedback sets how many echoes there are, and with none there is a single echo.

C7.5.q: Part of each echo is sent back into the delay. What does that give you?
options: A longer train of echoes, each quieter than the last
A single echo, a little louder than the note
A longer gap between one echo and the next
Echoes that follow the tempo of the click
C7.5.why: Feedback sends part of each echo back in to be echoed again, so more feedback gives a longer train.

C7.5.q: What happens when the delay time is made very short?
options: The echoes blur into a metallic flutter stuck to the note
The echoes stop and the note is left clean
The echoes get louder with every repeat
The echoes land exactly on every click
C7.5.why: Very short times stop sounding like separate echoes and colour the tone.

C7.5.q: Why set the delay time in beats?
options: The echoes die away more slowly
The echoes keep one fixed gap at any tempo
The delay makes more echoes for each note
The echoes stay in time when the tempo changes
C7.5.why: Set in beats, the delay time follows the tempo, so the echoes stay on the rhythm.

C7.5.q: Delay time is set to Half a beat and you play notes on the click. Where do the echoes land?
options: Exactly on top of each click
Just before each click
Exactly between the clicks
At a different place each time
C7.5.why: Set in beats, the delay time follows the tempo, so half a beat lands between the clicks.

C7.6.q: You play a few short notes, then switch on Reverb. What changes?
options: Each note is followed by one clear echo
Each note becomes brighter and buzzier
Each note rings on in a space after it stops
Each note takes longer to start
C7.6.why: Reverb is a dense wash of echoes that dies away, so each note rings on after it stops.

options: A few clear echoes spaced evenly in time
Thousands of echoes too close together to hear separately
Copies of the sound drifting slightly out of tune
One long echo that repeats on the beat
C7.6.why: Reverb is a dense wash of echoes from every surface, which then dies away.

C7.6.q: Which room's reverb takes longest to die away?
options: A small room with hard surfaces
A big room with soft surfaces
A big room with hard surfaces
A small room with soft surfaces
C7.6.why: The bigger and harder the room, the longer the wash of echoes takes to die away.

C7.6.q: You want a small, close room with only a short bloom after each note. What do you do?
options: Turn Size down
Turn Size up
Turn Mix up to 100%
Play a fast run of notes
C7.6.why: Size is how long the tail lasts, so a small Size gives a short bloom like a close room.

C7.6.q: You want the sound to seem further away, at the far end of the room. What do you do?
options: Turn Mix down
Turn Mix up
Turn Size up
Turn Size down
C7.6.why: Mix sets how far away the sound seems, and Size sets how long the tail lasts.

C7.6.q: Which kind of playing suits a long reverb best?
options: A fast run of short notes
Quick repeated notes with no gaps
Fast playing with Mix at full
Single notes with long gaps after them
C7.6.why: Long tails blur fast notes together, while a single note has room to ring.

C7.C.q: The hidden sound differs in the tone itself, not in what follows the note. Which effects do you check?
options: Delay or reverb
Distortion or EQ
Delay or EQ
Reverb or distortion
C7.C.why: A change in the tone itself points to distortion or EQ.

C7.C.q: After the note you hear separate repeats, not a smooth wash. Which effect is it?
options: A reverb
A distortion
An EQ
A delay
C7.C.why: Separate repeats are a delay, and a smooth wash is a reverb.

C7.C.q: How can you judge the hidden sound's delay time by ear?
options: Count how many echoes there are
Listen to how bright the echoes are
Count the gap between the echoes
Listen to how long the space rings
C7.C.why: The gap between echoes is the delay time, so counting it tells you the setting.
